listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to the audio edition for the week of the ninth. Three things before we start the sections. Our correspondent in Ankara has filed the briefing this week, and it runs a little longer than usual, so the finance pages have moved back by four. The editorial takes a position that some of you are not going to like, and we know that, because we ran a version of the same argument in March and the letters came in for a month. And finally, a correction. Last week we said the vote was on the twelfth. It was on the twenty-first. The error was ours and not the correspondent's, and we apologize for it.

Here is what actually works with a difficult article, and it takes twenty minutes a week rather than an hour a day. Start at the end. Read the last paragraph first, because in this kind of writing the last paragraph is where the argument lands, and once you know where you are going the middle stops being a fog. Then go back to the top and skim, not for meaning but for shape. The names, the numbers, the two or three words that come back three times. Only now read it properly, and while you read, keep one question in your head. What is this writer trying to make me believe? Then mark one sentence you disagree with, even slightly. That one sentence is the thing you will be able to say out loud at a table on Friday, and saying it is the whole point. Finishing the magazine is not.

extra_audio.text: Ruth notices that Braulio has had the same page open for twenty minutes, and asks him whether the language is the problem. He answers that it is not the language, and that what slows him down is everything the sentence decides not to say. Ruth tells him that the editorial is where the opinion lives, and that it carries no name at the bottom on purpose. Braulio suggests that what he should do is skim the whole thing first and then choose one piece. Ruth agrees, and admits that it was that habit that got her through twenty years of reading for a living.

reading.rtitle: The Magazine You Are Not Supposed to Finish
paras: Nobody reads the whole thing. That is worth saying first, because most people who give up on a serious weekly give up out of guilt rather than out of difficulty. A subscription buys you about a hundred pages every seven days, and the reader the editors have in mind is not a reader who finishes. It is a reader who chooses.

The shape of the magazine tells you where to choose. The first pages carry the editorial, which is the opinion of the publication itself and not of any single writer, which is exactly why it carries no name at the bottom. Behind it sits the briefing, a longer piece that gives you the background on one story and assumes you know nothing about it. Then come the country sections, written by a correspondent who lives there, and those are the pages where the reporting actually lives.

The difficulty is rarely the vocabulary. It is that a good deal of the meaning is never stated. A sentence makes an assertion in eight words and leaves the implication to you. Half a paragraph later something inconvenient is glossed over inside a subordinate clause, with a caveat attached to it so quietly that you almost miss the retreat. To scrutinize every line is the wrong instinct, because you would never reach the end. What works is to skim first for shape, then read one piece properly, and draw the inference yourself.

There is one more habit worth stealing from the writing. The editors do not simply disagree with the people they cover. They refute them, which means they take the claim, name it, and put the evidence against it, in that order. It is that move, far more than the vocabulary, that makes the writing sound authoritative. Notice it on the page and you will start hearing it at dinner tables.
reading.source: Article -- The Reader's Column, a weekly newsletter about the press
